recent.question: Kentucky wins
recent.what_happened: No. 25 Kentucky beat No. 10 LSU 35-34 in overtime at Kroger Field. Kentucky tied the game with a late field goal, answered Leavitt's overtime touchdown with a Baxter TD, then won on a two-point conversion. A 55-yard punt-return touchdown also helped.
recent.what_we_missed: Nothing decisive was missed. The forecast of 0.32 was already above the market's 0.255, leaning toward the home underdog. The game came down to a two-point try in overtime, which is close to a coin flip.
recent.lesson: For ranked home underdogs in conference play, a moderate lean above the market price is reasonable, but don't move further on the strength of outcomes decided by one-score overtime results.

suggested_change.change: No process change is needed. The forecast leaned the right way relative to the market, and the outcome came down to a late-game coin flip.

recent.question: UNLV wins
recent.what_happened: UNLV beat previously unbeaten North Dakota State 13-7 at Allegiant Stadium on Oct 10, 2026. UNLV's defense shut out the Bison in the second half. NDSU QB Nathan Hayes threw three interceptions, one returned for a touchdown, and coach Tim Polasek's fourth-down tries at the UNLV 4-yard line and at NDSU's own 18 both failed.
recent.what_we_missed: Nothing that could have been known beforehand decided this game. The result came down to turnovers and failed fourth downs in a low-scoring game. Our forecasts (0.37–0.41) were a little below the market's 0.445, and the market had better credited UNLV's home field and NDSU's first year in FBS.
recent.lesson: When a FCS-to-FBS newcomer is unbeaten against a weak schedule and plays an FBS home team, don't move further from the market than it already is, because the newcomer's record may overstate its strength.

suggested_change.change: No process change is needed. This was a close game, and the less likely result happened because of turnovers.

recent.question: North Dakota St. wins
recent.what_happened: UNLV won 13-7 at home at Allegiant Stadium. NDSU's defense held up, but its offense scored only one touchdown, in the second quarter, and was shut out in the second half. That ended the Bison's 5-0 start.
recent.what_we_missed: Nothing decisive. The 0.58 forecast was slightly above the market's 0.555, likely because of NDSU's 5-0 record and No. 1 scoring defense. It didn't fully weigh that NDSU was a road team in its first FBS season with an offense that hadn't been tested by FBS defenses, or that NDSU's only game against a solid opponent was a close 38-32 win over Air Force.
recent.lesson: For a near-coin-flip road game, stay close to the market price unless you have specific new information. A strong record built mostly against weak or FCS opponents doesn't justify moving above the market.

suggested_change.change: The forecast was well calibrated and near the market price. A 42% outcome happening is normal variance, so no process change is needed.

recent.question: North Dakota St. wins by over 3.5 points
recent.what_happened: UNLV beat North Dakota State 13-7 at Allegiant Stadium. The Bison scored only in the second quarter and were shut out in the second half, so the bet on NDSU winning by more than 3.5 points lost.
recent.what_we_missed: Before kickoff, the market and the models all called this close to a coin flip: ESPN FPI gave UNLV a 51.9% chance to win, Dimers projected NDSU 25-23, and the market priced NDSU covering at 42.5%. The research leaned on NDSU's 5-0 record and +23 average margin, which mostly came against weak opponents, and gave little weight to the fact that this was a first-year FBS team playing a road game against a decent home FBS opponent.
recent.lesson: If the market price and public models such as FPI agree on a near pick'em, don't move 25 points away from them because of a team's raw win-loss record and average margin unless you have specific information they lack.

suggested_change.change: For sports spread markets, always pull the betting line and at least one public model (FPI, SP+ or Dimers), and cap how far the forecast can stray from that consensus unless there is concrete news to justify it.

recent.question: Will IK Oddevold win on 2026-10-10?
recent.what_happened: Oddevold won the home game against Nordic United in regular time, so the market resolved YES. I couldn't find the score or a match report. Every source my search turned up was a preview.
recent.what_we_missed: The market put Oddevold at 55.5%, and prediction sites gave them about 60%. The forecaster's 37% went well below that because of Oddevold's high draw rate and modest home form. It gave too little weight to Nordic United's poor defending (12 goals conceded in their last five games, including three home defeats). The two sides were level on points, and that kind of evidence doesn't justify an 18-point gap from the market.
recent.lesson: If your own statistics are mixed and point both ways, don't move more than about 10 points away from a liquid market price unless you have specific news the market lacks, such as injuries or lineups.

suggested_change.change: Require a named, specific piece of information before placing a bet against the market when the forecast is more than 10 points from the market price on a low-information league match.

recent.question: Will the highest temperature in Wellington be 20°C on October 10?
recent.what_happened: The question resolved YES: NZWN's highest reading on 10 Oct 2026 was 20°C, 2–3°C above the 17–18°C that consumer forecast sites were giving. I couldn't find a news or observation record explaining why it ran warm.
recent.what_we_missed: Our evidence was two consumer forecast snippets (17°C and 18°C) plus a few years of October climate figures. We had no MetService or model ensemble spread, and nothing on how warm the northerly flow might get. Even so, 0.19 matched the market's 0.20, so the information we had did not point clearly to 20°C.
recent.lesson: Under northerly flow, Wellington Airport highs often come in several degrees above the point forecasts on consumer sites. Build a ±2–3°C error spread around the forecast high rather than putting most of the probability on the forecast value and the bracket either side of it.

suggested_change.change: For Wellington temperature markets, pull MetService's official forecast and model ensemble spreads, and check past forecast error for the airport station under the expected wind direction, instead of relying on aggregator snippets.

recent_wins.question: Cleveland wins
recent_wins.what_happened: Cleveland beat the White Sox 2-0 in ALDS Game 5 at Progressive Field on Oct 10, 2026, coming back from 0-2 down in the series. Gavin Williams struck out 12, tying the franchise record, and José Ramírez hit a two-run homer in the 4th, the only runs of the game.
recent_wins.what_worked: With research the forecaster said 64%, against 56.5% for the market and 34% without research. It correctly picked out home field, Cleveland's momentum after Games 3 and 4, Williams as the likely starter with his AL-leading strikeout numbers and 11 strikeouts in Game 2, and a tired White Sox bullpen. Still, a single winner-take-all baseball game at 64% is close to a coin flip, and a 2-0 game could easily have gone the other way.
recent_wins.lesson: In single-elimination baseball games, treat a starter edge plus home field as a small move of a few points over the market, and size bets to match rather than calling it strong evidence.

suggested_change.change: Limit bet size when our probability is within about 10 points of a market priced between 40% and 60% on a single MLB game, since the result is mostly variance.

recent_wins.question: Marshall wins by over 4.5 points
recent_wins.what_happened: The question resolved NO: Marshall did not win the October 10, 2026 home game against Coastal Carolina by more than 4.5 points. I could not find the final score, so I can't say whether Marshall won narrowly, pushed toward the line, or lost.
recent_wins.what_worked: With research, the forecast came down to 0.28 from about 0.40. Several facts pushed it lower: Marshall had won its three games by 2, 6 and 1 points; it allowed 35 points a game while Coastal Carolina allowed 25; Coastal's three recent losses were all close; and Coastal had won 3 of the last 4 meetings. Still, the market's 0.495 put the line at roughly a fair spread, and covering a 4.5-point spread in college football is close to a coin flip, so most of the edge here was luck rather than proven skill.
recent_wins.lesson: When a spread market is priced near 50%, close margins in a team's wins plus a defense that gives up a lot of points are reasonable reasons to lean against the favorite covering. Size those bets modestly, because one game's margin is very noisy.

suggested_change.change: Cap the stake on spread-cover bets where the market is between 0.45 and 0.55 and the edge comes only from season-margin stats, unless the research turned up something like an injury or a quarterback change that the line hasn't priced in.

recent_wins.question: Will Atlanta United FC win on 2026-10-10?
recent_wins.what_happened: FC Cincinnati won 3-1 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on Oct 10, 2026, with two goals from Kévin Denkey and a late one from Tom Barlow; Miguel Almirón scored Atlanta's only goal. Cincinnati won even without Evander, and the market resolved No.
recent_wins.what_worked: The researched forecast of 0.27, against a market price of 0.425 and 0.39 without research, rested on base rates. Atlanta had only 3 wins in their last 10 home games and sat 28th in the league. Cincinnati had lost just 1 of the last 9 meetings and had a decent record at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. The forecast also accounted for the fact that a draw counts as No. Cincinnati's five-game winless run and Evander's absence didn't outweigh those factors. Still, this is one match: even at the market's price, No was about 58% likely, so a fair share of this result was variance.
recent_wins.lesson: When a home team's own home record is poor and the head-to-head trend is lopsided, don't let it get credit for home advantage just for playing at home. Remember that the draw also pays No when the market prices a weak favorite above 40%.

suggested_change.change: Pull the home team's recent home-only record and the last 8–10 head-to-head results as standard inputs for single-match soccer win markets. Weigh them against the market's implied home advantage before reacting to injury news.

recent_wins.question: Will Manchester United FC win on 2026-10-10?
recent_wins.what_happened: The match at Old Trafford finished Manchester United 1–1 Tottenham. Mbeumo put United ahead in the 73rd minute, Bentancur was sent off, and Solanke headed in a 90+2 equaliser for 10-man Spurs, so the market resolved No.
recent_wins.what_worked: We put United at 0.43 against a market price of 0.565. That rested on real points: United had one win in five league games, a long injury list (Sesko, Dorgu, De Ligt, Ugarte, with Rashford, Mainoo and Amad doubtful), a poor recent record against Spurs, and a draw-prone Spurs side that kept clean sheets in two 0–0 games. Still, United led until stoppage time, so this No came from one late header and was close to a coin flip.
recent_wins.lesson: When a struggling favourite at home is priced above 55% to win, remember a draw also resolves No, and price it in explicitly (roughly 25–30% here) rather than letting the opponent's place in the table anchor the estimate.

suggested_change.change: Have the researcher give an explicit three-way estimate (win, draw, loss) from bookmaker odds or recent draw rates, so the gap with the market comes from stated numbers rather than a gut discount.

recent_wins.question: Will AFC Bournemouth win on 2026-10-10?
recent_wins.what_happened: Chelsea beat Bournemouth 5-1 at Stamford Bridge on 10 October 2026, so the question resolved No. Chelsea led 2-0 inside three minutes through Henderson and Rogers, João Pedro scored twice and Henderson added a late goal. Bournemouth are still without a Premier League win under Marco Rose after six matchdays.
recent_wins.what_worked: Research pulled the forecast down from 0.38 to 0.11, well below the market's 0.205. It found Bournemouth with no wins and a long list of injuries (Scott, Kluivert, Brooks, Kroupi and possibly Gittens), Chelsea's key players (Caicedo, Palmer, James, João Pedro) declared fit, and Chelsea unbeaten in 9 meetings. To be fair, the market also made No about an 80% favourite, so the edge over the market was modest. The lopsided score backs the research, but on its own it doesn't prove 0.11 was the better number.
recent_wins.lesson: When an away underdog is winless and missing several first-choice attackers while the home side gets its stars back, size the forecast mainly from the team news, not from the home side's recent form or leaky defence.

suggested_change.change: Always compare the two sides' injury and availability lists from the latest press conferences before forecasting a match, because here they mattered more than the head-to-head history or recent results.

recent_wins.question: Will Brentford FC win on 2026-10-10?
recent_wins.what_happened: The VAVEL live blog reported Aston Villa 2-2 Brentford at Villa Park on 10 October 2026, with Brentford equalising late after Villa led. That source's headline still showed 1-1, so the exact score isn't fully confirmed. Either way Brentford did not win in 90 minutes, so the market resolved No.
recent_wins.what_worked: With research, the forecast dropped to 27%, below the market's 37.5%. It gave weight to Brentford's away record (three straight away league draws, no away win since February), injuries to Collins, van den Berg, Jensen and Damsgaard, Ouattara being ill, and the usual low chance of an away win at a Champions League side with a strong home record. It did not let Brentford's 4th place or last season's two 1-0 wins over Villa push it up.
recent_wins.lesson: For away-win markets, start from the roughly 25-30% base rate for a mid-table side visiting a stronger home team, and only move up from there on concrete evidence. A good early-season league position or one lucky past meeting is not enough, and draws count as No.

rules.rule: Read crypto rules for the exact strike, venue/pair (e.g. Binance BTC/USDT) and test (any touch or a close at a set candle), restate the strike up top, measure each price fact against it, and record a timestamped spot from that venue under an hour old for same-day windows.

For crypto threshold questions, report percent distance to strike, hours left, how many of the last 14 days the venue traded through that level, realized volatility, any weekend, and timestamped same-day catalysts (yields, dollar, ETF flows, jobs data) or state none found.

When judged mid-window, first check whether the strike was already reached inside the window: cite dated reports of the high and its margin past the strike, confirm on the resolution venue's candles where possible, and treat earlier-week moves as background.

For match questions, report both sides' dated absences and returns from the latest press conferences, the stand-in and the absent player's actual recent output, settled from confirmed lineups; label all-time series and head-to-heads under about 10 games as weak.
Discard any search snippet claiming a match result that is undated or dated before kickoff; report a result only from sources published after the match was played.

For game-total questions (goals or points), report both teams' recent game totals with dates, label a 3–4 game streak as a small sample, note weakened opponents in any blowout, and report each side's starting QB or key starter changes and defensive ranking.

For tennis completion questions, read which endings count, report the tour level's normal-finish share and each player's recent full matches, weigh only past-week injury or withdrawal news, and after start time check Tennis Explorer or ITF for w/o or ret. first.

For NFL player props, research the named player, never team D/ST rates: for TDs, his TDs per game this and last season, red-zone carries or targets and target share; for yardage, attempts per game and games past the line; plus the opponent's rank and injured defenders.

For single MMA fights, report each fighter's age, recent opponents and how those fights ended, and dated weigh-in or weight-cut news; label win streaks and common-opponent comparisons as weak evidence.

For single MLB games, report confirmed starters' ERA, ERA+ and recent starts, each bullpen's unavailable arms (injury, leave, short rest), season and road records, and form since Sept 1; label old-roster franchise streaks and series-level rates as not single-game evidence.

For playoff series, first get the live or final score of any game started before the judgment time, then report the series score, wins the trailer needs and where, the cited comeback rate for that deficit, game margins and season records; past seasons' playoffs are background.

For in-round golf leader questions, pull the live hole-by-hole leaderboard and, for the named player and everyone within about 3 shots, report score, holes left and tee wave, plus the field's scoring average and how the rules settle a tie for the lead.

For golf tournament winner questions, report the player's world ranking, pro starts and wins, the field's strength and size, and his prior-week schedule (e.g. a team event); label team-event results and a single pro win as weak evidence of dominance.

For video view questions, check the channel's uploads since the question opened and report any new video's upload time, hours elapsed, views and climb rate first; build references only from first-168-hour counts of recent comparable uploads, not lifetime or undated totals.

For live-streamed challenge questions near the deadline, get the current attempt's status from the past 12 hours (stream VODs, streamers' socials, fan trackers): milestones reached, gear, deaths or resets, plus the participants' own past completions and times.

For Rotten Tomatoes score questions, read the year-specific film page named in the rules, record the score, review count and dated earlier readings showing drift, and count how many negative reviews would move it past the strike before the check time.

For reality-show elimination questions, confirm every fact names the asked contestant and their own pro partner, and report couples left, eliminations per episode, live shows in the window, and every couple's judges' scores and bottom-three history.

For multi-seat or multi-candidate elections, report alongside polls the undecided share, joint tickets and endorsements, late dropouts and whom they backed, whether one side's vote splits across candidates, and dated past gaps between final polls and results there.

Take counts and base rates from a cited source covering the current format to the latest event, using the resolution's named provider and its counting method first (e.g. its trailing 2–4 weeks); label recalled, disputed or roughly dozen-case counts as unverified.

proposals.title: Find out why Sharp line has never bet

Either its price feed never matches our markets or its 3c edge and 20-85c price band filter out everything. Without bets we can't learn whether a sharp bookmaker line beats the prediction-market price.

retro.headline: A quiet half-day: few bets settled, every Jev and Claude strategy except Jev + research is locked until 14-17 October, and ch16 (sports-only Claude) is still the only strategy in profit, at +$4.8k on just 6 settled bets.
went_well: ch16 (Claude direct, sports only) is up $4.8k all time, winning 4 of 6 settled bets, all priced 30-60c. Since its info gate dropped to 0.2 it is +$6.8k on 5 settled, with 21 still open. That is an experiment, not a finding.
Favourites (60c and up) have paid for calibrated (8 of 8, +$5.9k) and main (3 of 3, +$2.2k). Bold lost $4.6k on 19 such bets, so this is mixed evidence across 30 bets.

Claude direct is nearly level with the market on measured skill (raw -0.0005 on 640 markets). In sports it beats the market outright, with Brier 0.167 against 0.181 on 169 markets. It is the closest any forecaster gets.
went_badly: We still don't beat the market. On 640 paired markets the market scores Brier 0.162 (lower is better); Claude direct scores 0.201 and Jev + research 0.218. Every lambda is 0, so all sizing is still small probe bets.

On the shared markets main and original both bet on (the 'yardstick'), main loses $35 per $100 staked against original's $18 (24 vs 37 settled). Since main raised its minimum edge to 12c it has lost both settled bets (-$3.3k on 2; too few to judge).
Coin-flip bets (30-60c) lose money for every Jev strategy: bold -$6.2k on 57, calibrated -$8.7k on 16, main -$2.3k on 18. The 30c floor stopped the long-shot bleeding but has not made money.

Bold's info-gate test has told us little: markets stopped only by that gate lose about the same as bets placed (-$31 vs -$31 per $100 on 167 and 62), so bold's slot is better spent testing whether Jev + research can earn in its best category. This is an experiment.

ideas_for_joey.title: Break results down by price paid
ideas_for_joey.why: Many losses, including all 3 of claude_direct's and every info-gate-stopped group, show -$100 per $100, meaning the whole stake was lost. That pattern suggests we may be buying cheap longshots. A breakdown of wins and P&L by ask price (for example <0.2, 0.2–0.5, 0.5–0.8, >0.8), for placed and stopped bets, would let us set min_ask and max_ask from evidence instead of guessing.

ideas_for_joey.title: Score forecasters on 30c+ markets only
ideas_for_joey.why: Since 2026-10-01 every strategy bets only at 30c or more, but the Brier table (market 0.114 vs our best 0.121) mixes in the long shots we no longer touch. We need to know whether any forecaster beats the price where we actually bet, matched market by market.

ideas_for_joey.title: Shrink forecasts toward the market before computing edge
ideas_for_joey.why: The market's Brier (0.123, 201 markets) beats every forecaster, and most of our losses came from bets where we disagreed with it most, such as long shots that went 1 for 21. A strategy option that blends the forecast with the market price (for example 50/50) before the edge check would bet only where a disagreement survives that discount. The forecasters themselves would still never see the price.

ideas_for_joey.title: Gate ledger and price breakdown for 30c+ markets only
ideas_for_joey.why: The gate ledger mixes in long shots, which lost 1 in 42 before the floor. That makes every 'stopped by the info gate' number look worse than it would under today's rules: calibrated's info-stopped markets show −$7.1 per $100 (66) and main's −$24.6 (78). We can't sensibly tune the info gates until the ledger shows only markets the 30c floor would let through.

ideas_for_joey.title: Pooled tally of bets placed under the floor
ideas_for_joey.why: Each strategy has 0–1 settled bets since 2026-10-01, so the floor's '30 settled bets' test will take weeks per strategy. Pooling every strategy's 30c+ bets placed since the floor, measured against original's long shots over the same period, would answer whether the floor pays much sooner.

ideas_for_joey.title: Claimed edge vs realised return
ideas_for_joey.why: Every source is worse than the market, yet each bet claims at least 8c of edge. Bucketing settled 30c+ bets by claimed edge (8-12c, 12-20c, 20c+) and showing win rate and P&L per $100 would show whether big claimed edges are real edges or big errors. That would tell us whether to raise or lower min_edge.

ideas_for_joey.title: Calibrated vs main on the same markets
ideas_for_joey.why: Calibrated's profit (+$3.4k on 9 settled since the floor) contrasts with its Brier of 0.210, slightly worse than raw Jev + research at 0.2065. So its edge may come from which bets it picks and how it sizes them, or it may be luck. A paired comparison would show whether the calibration itself earns money before anyone considers moving main onto it.

ideas_for_joey.title: Price breakdown since each strategy's last rule change
ideas_for_joey.why: by_price_paid is all-time, so pre-floor long shots dominate it: about $100k of losses on 73 bets. That hides whether 30-60c and 60c+ bets pay under the current rules. Bold's -$5.5k and calibrated's +$5.0k in favourites can't be dated to a rule version.

ideas_for_joey.title: Report settled stake separately from open stake
ideas_for_joey.why: Most of our judge_by tests use 'P&L per $100 staked since the change', but the reported stake includes open bets. Bold has 14 of 41 bets open and ch16 has 8 of 10, so the per-$100 figures look better than they are. Splitting settled stake from open stake would let us judge p14, p18, p19, p21, p23 and p24 honestly.

ideas_for_joey.title: Measure skill per category as well as per source
ideas_for_joey.why: Claude's pooled edge over the market is negative (-0.020 on 564 markets), which keeps ch16 on probe bets forever, even though Claude beats the market in sports (0.167 vs 0.178 on 152). Measuring lambda for each source and category pair, with the same 300-market threshold, would let a real pocket of skill size up without loosening the rule anywhere else.

ideas_for_joey.title: Find out why Sharp line has never bet
ideas_for_joey.why: The Sharp (Pinnacle) strategy shows 0 bets, 0 open and n=0 in the skill table, while every other source has hundreds of judged markets. Either its price feed never matches our markets or its 3c edge and 20-85c price band filter out everything. Without bets we can't learn whether a sharp bookmaker line beats the prediction-market price.

ideas_for_joey.title: Sanity-check the skill estimate before it drives sizing
ideas_for_joey.why: Every source shows a standard error of exactly 0.0. Sharp line shows raw skill 23.593 on just 7 markets, while the others sit around -0.03, so the scale looks wrong. If lambda turns positive with a bad error estimate or a bad scale, Kelly sizing could bet far too much.

ideas_for_joey.title: Yardstick split since main's last rule change
ideas_for_joey.why: Main's 12c-edge test (p23) is to be judged on yardstick P&L for bets opened after 2026-10-07. The report only gives the yardstick since 2026-09-29: main -$17.4k on 24 settled, original -$15.9k on 37. Those figures mix old rules with new.
